title.en: Atomic models, subatomic particles and electron arrangement

text.en: Early scientists pictured the atom as a solid ball. Experiments showed instead a tiny dense nucleus with electrons around it, rather like planets around the Sun.

Atoms contain protons (positive charge, in the nucleus), neutrons (no charge, in the nucleus) and electrons (negative charge, moving around the nucleus).
Dalton thought of atoms as indivisible; Thomson proposed the plum-pudding model; Rutherford discovered the dense positive nucleus using alpha particles; Bohr proposed electrons in fixed orbits.
Atomic number Z = number of protons (= number of electrons in a neutral atom); mass number A = protons + neutrons.
Electrons fill shells K, L, M, N with capacities 2, 8, 18 and 32 (2n squared).
Sodium (Z = 11) has the arrangement 2, 8, 1, and chlorine (Z = 17) has 2, 8, 7.
Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers; isobars have the same mass number but different atomic numbers.
Valency is the combining capacity of an atom, determined by the outer-shell electrons.

text.en: 12 electrons fill K = 2, L = 8, then M = 2.
